title: Draw and Measure
big_idea: Be exact to the nearest centimetre
child_idea: A ruler counts centimetres. Start at the 0 mark, read the mark at the other end, and draw or measure a line exactly.

topics: Measuring a line to the nearest cm
Drawing a line of a given length
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only (MOE Measurement, length in cm, 1.1 to 1.4). It is not a claim that the program covers the school syllabus, and it must not appear on child or parent pages as 'MOE-aligned'. Deeper than the holiday cubes-and-ruler lesson, which is warm-up only.

contest_moves: a bent path: add the straight pieces
a line that starts at a mark other than 0 (end mark take away start mark)
cutting a ribbon into pieces (the total stays the same)
objectives: Use a ruler correctly: put the 0 mark at the start, keep it straight, read the mark at the other end.
Draw a straight line of a given whole number of centimetres, up to 14 cm.
Measure to the nearest centimetre: when the end is between two marks, choose the closer mark.
Compare two lengths and say how much longer one is.
Find the length of a line that starts at a mark other than 0, and of a bent path made of straight pieces.

remember: Measure with same-size things laid end to end, no gaps and no overlaps, then count them
Find 0 on a ruler and count along the marks to 12
A centimetre (cm) is the gap from one mark to the next
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20. A child who has never used a ruler is shown 0, the marks and the gaps with their own ruler in the warm-up. Nothing from earlier Term 1 lessons is needed. If the child has done the holiday measuring lesson, laying things end to end and reading cm will feel familiar.
holiday_topics_revisited: Measuring with cubes and a ruler (Measure It!)
joining_cold.note: This lesson stands alone: it needs no earlier lesson except through the warm-up. It is one of the safer Term 1 lessons to miss (plan: the safest is Lesson 4). A child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 with a ruler before Lesson 10.

child: A ruler with cm marks, starting at 0 (15 or 30 cm)
3 or 4 things to measure; 10 paper clips (or small same-size things)
Workbook pages 1 to 5 (A4; page 6 is not used), a pencil, a rubber, spare paper
tutor: A real ruler, a pencil and a strip of paper to show on camera; a phone or camera that can look down at the table
A visible clock or a timer slide
materials.notes: Families keep a ruler at home, so no ruler is printed in the workbook. If a child has none, a grown-up can look for any straight-edged ruler or strip marked in centimetres, or tell the tutor before the lesson. Plastic or wooden rulers only, no metal edges. Nothing needs to be bought. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears.

workbook.hint_p1: Use your ruler and a pencil. Say your answer out loud, then write it.
workbook.hint_p3: Use your ruler and a drawing. Then write how you know. Choose any question, in any order.

timing.notes: A 4-minute opening: greeting, the ruler check (everyone shows the 0 end to the camera), the recording notice and a hands-apart estimate. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide and the spare-time menu are used only if the lesson is on time.

sneak_peek.q1: Draw a dot. Now draw a line from the dot that is exactly 3 cm long. Use your ruler.
sneak_peek.q2: Ali puts the end of a pencil at the 1 mark on his ruler. The tip is at the 9 mark. Ali says: it is 9 cm long. Is he right? Write yes or no, and why.
sneak_peek.a1: A line from the dot that is 3 cm long: the 0 mark on the dot and the 3 mark at the other end.
sneak_peek.a2: No. It is 8 cm long. The pencil starts at the 1 mark, not the 0 mark, so the first centimetre of the ruler is not part of the pencil (9 take away 1 is 8).

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, your workbook and your ruler. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your ruler, workbook, pencil and paper. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Lay clips along a pencil, find 0 on your ruler, and count the marks out loud. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Do each step with your own ruler before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your own paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Guess, then measure three things. Then draw lines of 3, 8 and 12 centimetres. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Guess and measure three things, then draw each line with your ruler. Write what you find.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy each example with your own ruler. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the examples with your ruler. Rewind any step you missed.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Big jump for ten centimetres, small hop for one.
break.action: Stand up and jump the tens and hop the ones.

work.say: Recording: pause now and do workbook page 1 with your ruler. When you finish a page, press play to check it.
work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

talk.say: Recording: pause. Tell a grown-up your answer to the talk question, and say why.
talk.action: Pause. Explain your answer to someone at home, with a reason.

exit.say: Recording: pause and do the exit ticket on your own, with your ruler. Then press play to check it.
exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

look.say: Recording: pause and fill in your look-back box. You can pass.
look.action: Pause. Fill in the look-back box, or pass.

flex.say: Recording: well done for finishing! Show a grown-up one thing you found out.
flex.action: Show a grown-up your workbook and tell them one thing you found out.

lines.text: @rec

Good morning, inquirers! Cameras on, pencil ready, and your ruler on the table. This lesson is recorded so that a friend who is away can catch up. We record me and the screen only. You may switch your camera off whenever you like.
Greet each child by first name. Ask everyone to hold their ruler up to the camera for a moment so you can see the 0 end. Remind them: a ruler stays flat on the table, and it is only for measuring.
Here is a question to start. How long is a pencil? Show me with your two hands, as far apart as you think. Hold still.
Children show a guess with their hands. Say what you see in general (some wide, some narrow). Nobody is right or wrong yet.
Hands are not very exact. My hands and your hands are not the same size. Today we learn to measure and to draw lines exactly, so that everybody gets the same answer.
Let us warm up.

Ruler check: if a child has no ruler, a grown-up can look for any straight-edged ruler or strip marked in centimetres; do not ask the child to guess. No names on screen. Keep the greeting short and warm. Tell the group again that recordings show only you and the screen.
@rec
Get your pencil and your paper clips, or small things that are all the same size. Lay them end to end along your pencil. No gaps. No overlaps. Then count them.
Children lay clips (or pasta, short straws) along a pencil and count them.
How many clips long is your pencil? Say your number or show it on your fingers.

My pencil is 6 big clips long. Now I use small clips: 9. Same pencil, different numbers! The clips are not the same size. So people agree to use one unit that is the same for everybody: the centimetre.
Now your ruler. Find the 0 mark. Put your finger on it. Count along the marks with me: 0, 1, 2, 3, all the way to 10.
Count the marks together, pointing with a finger, from 0 to 10, then on to 12.
Which mark comes just after 4?
Which mark comes just before 10?
The space between two marks is one centimetre. We write it cm. From 0 to 1 is 1 cm. Slide your finger from 0 to 5. Five gaps: that is 5 cm.
Slide your finger from 0 to 8. How many centimetres is that?

A child who counts the marks instead of the gaps (says 6 for 0 to 5): put a finger on the 0 and say zero, then count each jump aloud: one, two, three, four, five. The 0 is where we start, it is not a centimetre.

Answers: any clip count is fine (the number depends on the clips). Then 5, 9, 8. Children answer with fingers, hands or a whispered number. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20 and a ruler.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Draw a dot. Now draw a line from the dot that is exactly 3 cm long. Use your ruler.
Children draw the dot and the 3 cm line on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Ali puts the end of a pencil at the 1 mark on his ruler. The tip is at the 9 mark. Ali says: it is 9 cm long. Is he right? Write yes or no, and why.
Children write or draw their answer.
Everyone holds their paper to the camera at the same moment, once, after puzzle two. Do not read answers aloud. No private chat.
Thank you. We will come back to puzzle two in a few minutes.

Puzzle 1 answer: a line 3 cm long (the 0 mark at the dot, the 3 mark at the other end). Puzzle 2 answer: no, 8 cm, because the pencil starts at the 1 mark. Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who started at 0, or who noticed the 1). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your ruler is your teacher. Find three things: a pencil, a spoon, an eraser or a toy. First guess how many centimetres long each one is. Then measure.
Put one end at the 0 mark, not at the edge of the ruler. Read the mark at the other end. If the end is between two marks, look which mark is closer.
Round 1: each child guesses, then measures three things. Tutor scans the cameras and asks a few children to hold their thing and ruler to the camera: look at the 0 end.
Tell me one of your things. My pencil is about how many centimetres? How close was your guess?
Round two: draw it! Put a dot. Put the 0 mark on the dot. Make a small mark at the end. Join the dot and the mark with a straight line. First, draw a line 3 cm long.
Children draw 3 cm.
Now draw a line 8 cm long.
Children draw 8 cm.
Now a line 12 cm long.
Children draw 12 cm.
On a count of three, everyone holds their paper to the camera. Look at where the lines start. No answers read aloud.
Ravi started his line at the very edge of his ruler, not at the 0 mark, and stopped at the 8 mark. Is his line exactly 8 cm? How do you know?
What did you notice? Where do we start measuring? What do we do if the end is between two marks?
We start at the 0 mark. We read the mark at the other end. If the end is between two marks, we choose the closer one. That is the nearest centimetre.

A child who measures from the edge of the ruler: ask them to find the 0 mark and slide the thing along until its end is on the 0. A child with a 15 cm ruler measuring something longer: ask them to measure a shorter thing, or mark the end of the ruler with a finger and slide on.
A child with nothing to measure: any straight line works, such as the edge of a book or a line they draw on paper.

Main room only: no breakout rooms in this lesson, so you can see every camera. Pairs are optional: a grown-up may check the 0 end. Ravi answer: no. He began a little before the 0 mark, so his line is a little longer than 8 cm. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Look at your ruler. The numbers sit on the marks. 0 is where we start. The gap from one mark to the next is one centimetre.
How many centimetres from the 0 mark to the 6 mark? Slide your finger and say it.
To measure: one end at 0, the ruler straight, and read the mark at the other end. Watch my pencil.
Show on camera: a pencil with its end exactly on the 0 mark, the ruler straight, read the tip aloud. Say the three steps while you do them.
To draw a line 7 cm long: a dot for the start. The 0 mark on the dot. A small mark at the 7. Then join them with a straight line. I draw while you watch.
Draw a 7 cm line on paper under the camera, saying each step. Check at the end: 0 at the start, 7 at the end.
Sometimes the end is not on a mark. Here it is between 8 and 9, and closer to 9. We say about 9 centimetres: the nearest centimetre.
Another one: between 12 and 13, and closer to 12. How long, to the nearest centimetre?
A line that does not start at 0. It starts at the 3 mark and ends at the 8 mark. Count the jumps: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. It is 5 cm long, not 8!
Why is it 5 cm and not 8 cm?
Your turn. Draw a line 5 cm long. Then: a line starts at the 2 mark and ends at the 9 mark. How long is it? Write both answers on your paper.
Children draw 5 cm and work out the second line.
The 5 cm line starts at 0 and ends at 5. The other line is 7 cm: count 7 jumps from 2 to 9, or take 2 from 9.

Key words every time: ruler, mark, centimetre (cm), start at 0, nearest. Do not teach millimetres or metres. Do not call the 0 a centimetre. The jump idea (count the gaps) is the same as hopping along a number line.

If a child draws from the end of the ruler: ask them to put a finger on the 0 mark and slide the ruler until the 0 is on the dot. If a child says the 2-to-9 line is 9 cm: ask them to count the jumps from the 2.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. We measure with our bodies today. A big jump is ten centimetres. A small hop is one centimetre. Fourteen centimetres is one big jump and four small hops.
Call 14, 23, 30, 8. Children jump the tens and hop the ones. Count the jumps and hops aloud together.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: draw a line 7 centimetres long. Start it at the 0 mark. Question 2: draw a line 4 cm long and a line 9 cm long. Which is longer, and by how much? Question 3: measure your pencil. Write your guess first.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Question 1: your line ends at the 7 mark. Question 2: the longer line is 9 cm, and it is 5 cm longer. Question 3: any measure close to your guess is fine. Mark your own page in another colour.
After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

Page 2. Question 4: Ali and Mei measure pencils. Question 5: draw a line 5 cm long, then a line 3 cm longer. Question 6: Mei says her line is 8 cm. Is she right? Question 7: the tip of Ben's spoon is between two marks.
Page 2, questions 4 to 7.
Question 4: 13 cm, 9 cm, and 4 cm longer. Question 5: 8 cm. Question 6: no, her line is 7 cm. Question 7: 15 cm.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.
Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page.

Q1 and Q2 (drawing): put a finger on the 0 mark, slide the ruler to the dot. Q3: guess first, then measure; a guess that is far off is fine. Q6: ask where her line ends on the ruler. Q7: which mark is the tip closer to?

A child who is still stuck ticks the stuck box on the look-back page. You check in during the open session in the next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). Never a private message.
Think harder is for ideas taught today in a new setting. Go further is for mastery and extension. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree.
@rec
Mei measures a pencil and says it is 15 cm. Ben measures the same pencil and says it is 16 cm. What could have happened? How can we find out who is right?
Think for a moment. Put a pencil next to your ruler and show your screen what you would do.
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Ali put his pencil at the 1 mark and the tip was at the 9 mark. He said 9 cm. The pencil is 8 cm long, because it starts at the 1, not at the 0.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.

Model answer: the tip may be between the 15 and the 16 mark, so one child chose the other mark; or one child did not start at the 0 mark. Check by measuring again with the 0 at the start and choosing the closer mark. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5. You may use your ruler.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Everyone holds their ticket to the camera at the same moment so only you see it. No private chat.
Question 1: your line starts at 0 and ends at 6. Question 2: 9 centimetres longer. Question 3: 7 centimetres, because 10 take away 3 is 7.
Check your own ticket in a different colour. Well done. I will stamp your inquiry journal.

Mark S, D or H in the tutor tracker (tutor only): S = secure on all three, D = developing (one wrong), H = needs help (two or three wrong). If D or H, plan two minutes of catch-up at the start of Lesson 10, in the open session, no names. Do not read out any child's result.
@rec
Look-back. Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. If you like, tick one thing to try next time. You can pass. Nobody reads it out.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5.
Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Story Steps: Read It Twice. You need only a pencil and paper. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time: a strip of paper is 10 cm long. You may cut it at the 1 mark, the 2 mark and so on. How many different places can you cut? And if the strip is 20 cm long?
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: 9 places for the 10 cm strip, 19 for the 20 cm strip (one fewer than the length, because we cannot cut at the two ends). If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3b) instead of rushing on.

slides.title: Draw and Measure

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Use a ruler to measure and to draw lines exactly.

slides.note: Lesson 9 of Term 1, 90 minutes. Objective: measure and draw lines to the nearest centimetre with a ruler. Time plan: opening 0 to 4, warm-up 4 to 10, sneak-peek 10 to 14, explore 14 to 28, mini-lesson 28 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Tell the group the lesson is recorded (you and the screen only) and that a child may keep the camera off.
slides.subtitle: Length: centimetres

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: measure with clips

items: Lay clips along your pencil, end to end.
No gaps. No overlaps.
Count the clips.

blocks.head: WHAT IF?
items: Your friend uses bigger clips. Will the number be the same?

slides.note: Children lay paper clips (or any same-size things) along a pencil and count them. This is a spiral review of measuring in equal steps (holiday topic) and it lets a new child join: they see how it is done before they try. Show on camera with big clips and then small clips: the same pencil gives two different numbers, so we need one unit that everybody shares. Say centimetre only at the end of the part.

slides.title: Find 0 on your ruler

blocks.text: Put your finger on the 0 mark. Count along the marks.
Say the numbers with me

slides.note: Every child puts a finger on the 0 mark of their own ruler and counts along with you: 0 to 10, then on to 12. The strip on screen shows the numbers only, the real ruler is the one the child holds. Quick questions: the mark after 4 is 5, the mark before 10 is 9, 12 comes after 10. Rulers with a gap before the 0 are normal: we start at the 0 mark, not at the edge.

slides.title: One centimetre

blocks.text: The gap between two marks is 1 cm.
Slide your finger from 0 to 5. How many gaps? How many cm?

slides.note: A centimetre (cm) is the gap from one mark to the next. From 0 to 5 is five gaps, so 5 cm. The 0 is where we start: it is not a centimetre. Answers to the quick questions: 0 to 8 is 8 cm, 0 to 10 is 10 cm. If a child says 6 for 0 to 5, they counted the marks: ask them to count the jumps.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Draw a dot.
Draw a line from the dot that is exactly 3 cm long.
Use your ruler.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Ali puts the end of a pencil at the 1 mark on his ruler.
The tip is at the 9 mark.
Ali says: it is 9 cm long. Is he right? Write yes or no, and why.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (a 3 cm line) is an access question: any child with a ruler can try it. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea: where the pencil starts matters. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Everyone holds the paper to the camera once, at the same moment, after puzzle 2; there is no private chat and no board in front of the group. Answers: a line 3 cm long; no, 8 cm (the pencil starts at the 1 mark). Do not reveal Puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list of who found it easy.

slides.title: Explore: guess, then measure

items: Find 3 things: a pencil, a spoon, an eraser or a toy.
Guess how many cm long each one is.
Put one end at the 0 mark. Read the mark at the other end.
Say: my ___ is about ___ cm.

blocks.head: WHAT IF?
items: The end is between two marks. Which mark is closer?

slides.note: Round 1, about 6 minutes. Objects first, little writing. Children guess, then measure three things from home. Ask a few children to hold the thing and the ruler to the camera: look at where the thing starts on the ruler (the 0 mark, not the edge). The what-if card is open to everyone from the start and no child is named for using it: it previews the nearest-centimetre idea in the mini-lesson. A child with a 15 cm ruler measures shorter things.

slides.title: Draw it!

items: Put a dot where the line starts.
Put the 0 mark on the dot.
Make a small mark at the end.
Join them with a straight line.
3 cm
8 cm
12 cm

slides.note: Round 2, about 5 minutes. Call each length and let children draw it. On a count of three they hold the paper to the camera: you can see where the lines start, not their exact length, so do not judge on camera. Then ask about Ravi, who started at the edge of the ruler and not at the 0 mark: his line is a little longer than 8 cm. Answers: any line drawn with the 0 mark at the start and the end mark at 3, 8 and 12.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: Where do we start measuring?
What do we do when the end is between two marks?
Why do we all use centimetres?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: start at the 0 mark, not at the edge; read the mark at the other end; when the end is between two marks choose the closer mark, which is the nearest centimetre; everybody uses the same unit so everybody gets the same answer (the clips gave different numbers). Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up.

slides.title: The parts of a ruler

blocks.head: REMEMBER
items: 0 is where we start.
The gap from one mark to the next is 1 cm.

slides.note: Hold your real ruler to the camera next to this slide. The numbers sit on the marks; the centimetre is the gap between two marks. Ask: how many centimetres from the 0 mark to the 6 mark? Answer: 6. Say the word mark every time, and say gap or jump for the centimetre.

slides.title: Measure: three steps

items: Put one end of the thing at the 0 mark.
Keep the ruler straight along the thing.
Read the mark at the other end. That is the length in cm.

blocks.text: Look from straight above

slides.note: Show the three steps on camera with a pencil, one end exactly on the 0 mark. Say each step as you do it. Read the mark at the tip aloud, with the unit: 14 cm, for example. Looking from straight above matters: from the side the marks seem to shift. Do not ask a child to demonstrate yet.

slides.title: Draw a line 7 cm long

items: Put a dot where the line starts.
Put the 0 mark on the dot.
Make a small mark at the 7.
Join them with a straight line.
Check: 0 at the start, 7 at the end.

slides.note: Draw the line on paper under your camera while you say the five steps. Hold the ruler still with one hand and draw along the edge with the other. At the end, check aloud: the 0 mark was on the dot and the 7 mark is at the other end. A line that is a little long is the most common slip: it usually means the line started at the edge of the ruler.

slides.title: Between two marks

blocks.text: The end is between the 8 mark and the 9 mark. It is closer to the 9 mark.

blocks.head: NEAREST CENTIMETRE
items: Choose the closer mark. This one is about 9 cm.

slides.note: Use a real pencil whose tip falls between two marks. When the tip is clearly closer to one mark, choose that mark: that is the nearest centimetre. Ask the second example: between 12 and 13, closer to 12: answer 12 cm. Today every example is clearly closer to one mark; do not set one exactly halfway.

slides.title: A line that starts at 3

blocks.text: The line starts at 3 and ends at 8. Count the jumps. 5 jumps. The line is 5 cm long.
8 take away 3 is 5

slides.note: A line from the 3 mark to the 8 mark: the numbers show six marks, but only five jumps between them. Count the jumps aloud: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The length is the end mark take away the start mark: 8 take away 3 is 5. It is not 8, because the first 3 cm of the ruler are not part of the line. Ask: why is it 5 cm and not 8 cm? Link back to puzzle 2 only after Talk time.

slides.title: Your turn

blocks.text: Write on your paper. About 1 minute

cols.head: DRAW
items: Draw a line 5 cm long.

cols.head: WORK OUT
items: A line starts at the 2 mark and ends at the 9 mark.
How long is it?

slides.note: Each child draws and writes on their own paper. Walk the cameras. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group. If a child finishes early, they may check the line by measuring it again, starting at a different mark.

slides.title: Check: your turn

cols.head: DRAW
items: The line starts at the 0 mark and ends at the 5 mark.

cols.head: WORK OUT
items: 9 take away 2 is 7.

slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. The 5 cm line: 0 at the start, 5 at the end. The second line is 7 cm: count 7 jumps from 2 to 9, or take 2 from 9. If a child wrote 9, ask them to count the jumps from the 2.

slides.title: Jump the tens, hop the ones

blocks.text: A big jump is 10 cm. A small hop is 1 cm.
14 cm is 1 big jump and 4 small hops. Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call each number and have children jump the tens and hop the ones; count the jumps and hops aloud. No equipment. Keep it gentle for small spaces. The big jump for ten links to bundles of ten from Lesson 1, but do not teach that link now.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. About 9 minutes. Use your ruler

slides.note: Read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then question 3. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. For question 3 a child may measure any pencil: the answer depends on the pencil. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children mark their own page in a different colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Question 3 depends on the pencil: a guess within a few centimetres of the measure is fine, and a new pencil is usually between 17 and 19 cm.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 7. About 9 minutes. Use your ruler

slides.note: Read question 6 aloud: it is a spot-the-mistake. Read question 7 aloud as well: the tip is between two marks. Children may check any answer by measuring their own pencil against the ruler.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. Question 6: no, her line ends at the 7 mark so it is 7 cm; she should draw on to the 8 mark. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Our idea in a new setting
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: MEI AND BEN MEASURE THE SAME PENCIL
items: Mei says 15 cm.
Ben says 16 cm.

blocks.text: What could have happened? How can we find out who is right?
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Then volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: the tip may be between the 15 and the 16 mark and the two children chose different marks, or one child did not start at the 0 mark. We can check by measuring again with the 0 at the start and choosing the closer mark. Repeat each child's answer in your own words for the recording.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: No! The pencil starts at the 1 mark, so it is 8 cm long: 9 take away 1.

slides.note: Reveal puzzle 2 now. The pencil starts at the 1 mark and ends at the 9 mark: eight jumps, so 8 cm. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone's earlier answer.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back. About 3 minutes

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. After the time everyone holds the ticket to the camera at the same moment, so only the tutor sees it (no private chat). Stamp the inquiry journal.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children check their own ticket in a different colour. Question 1: the line starts at 0 and ends at 6. Question 2: 15 take away 6 is 9. Question 3: 10 take away 3 is 7.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby); never a direct message. The Next time I will try row is optional; at the start of the next lesson you may say to the whole group: today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Story Steps: Read It Twice
You need a pencil and paper.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (stamps, the look-back). Do not start anything new. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional menu slide and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: how many cuts?

blocks.text: A strip of paper is 10 cm long. You may cut it at the 1 mark, the 2 mark and so on.
How many different places can you cut? What if the strip is 20 cm long?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Answer: 9 places for the 10 cm strip (the marks 1 to 9), and 19 places for the 20 cm strip. We cannot cut at the 0 mark or the 10 mark, because that is the end of the strip. Take two answers and move on.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: A line ends at the 9 mark. Is it always 9 cm long?
Draw a path with 3 straight pieces for your grown-up to measure
Show how to draw a line 9 cm long, in steps

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

start.text: Draw a line 7 cm long in the box. Put the 0 mark of your ruler at the start of the line.

parts.text: My line starts at the ___ mark and ends at the ___ mark.

start.answer: A line from the 0 mark to the 7 mark: it starts at 0, ends at the 7 mark and is 7 cm long
start.hint: Make a dot. Put the 0 mark on the dot. Make a small mark at the 7. Join them with a straight line.
start.solution: Put a dot for the start. Line up the 0 mark with the dot. Make a small mark at the 7. Join the dot and the mark with a straight line. The line ends at the 7 mark, so it is 7 cm long.
mistakes: Starting at the edge of the ruler instead of the 0 mark (the line comes out a little too long).
Drawing to the 8 mark because the 0 was counted as one.

start.text: Draw a line 4 cm long. Under it, draw a line 9 cm long.

parts.text: The longer line is ___ cm long.
It is ___ cm longer than the short line.

start.hint: Draw the short line first, then the long one under it. To see how much longer, count the cm from 4 to 9.
start.solution: The 9 cm line is the longer one. To find how much longer, count on from 4 to 9: that is 5 jumps. So it is 5 cm longer (9 take away 4 is 5).
mistakes: Writing 13 by adding the two lengths.
Starting the 9 cm line at a mark other than 0.

start.text: Measure your pencil. First write your guess. Then measure to the nearest cm.

parts.text: My guess: ___ cm
I measured: ___ cm
parts.ans: about 17 to 19 for a new pencil

start.answer: Any sensible measure; a new pencil is about 17 to 19 cm. Check: the 0 mark at one end, read the mark at the other end
start.hint: Put one end of the pencil at the 0 mark. Keep the ruler straight. Read the mark at the other end. If it is between two marks, choose the closer one.
start.solution: Put one end of the pencil on the 0 mark and keep the ruler straight. Read the mark at the other end. A new pencil is usually between 17 and 19 cm. If the tip is between two marks, write the closer one.
mistakes: Starting at the edge of the ruler instead of the 0 mark.
Writing the guess in the measure space, or leaving off the unit.

start.text: Ali's pencil and Mei's pencil both start at the 0 mark of a ruler. Ali's tip is at the 13 mark. Mei's tip is at the 9 mark.

parts.text: Ali's pencil is ___ cm long.
Mei's pencil is ___ cm long.
Ali's pencil is ___ cm longer.

start.answer: 13 cm; 9 cm; Ali's is 4 cm longer
start.hint: Both pencils start at 0, so the mark at the tip is the length. To find how much longer, count on from 9 to 13.
start.solution: Both start at the 0 mark, so each tip mark is the length: Ali 13 cm, Mei 9 cm. From 9 to 13 is 4 jumps (13 take away 9 is 4), so Ali's pencil is 4 cm longer.
mistakes: Adding 13 + 9 = 22.
Writing 9 as the difference (that is the length of Mei's pencil).

start.text: Draw a line 5 cm long. Under it, draw a line that is 3 cm longer.

parts.text: The second line is ___ cm long.

start.answer: The second line is 8 cm long (5 + 3)
start.hint: The second line is the first line and 3 more. How long is that? Draw it with the 0 mark at the start.
start.solution: The first line is 5 cm. 3 cm longer is 5 + 3 = 8 cm. Draw it from the 0 mark to the 8 mark, under the first line.
mistakes: Drawing a line 3 cm long.
Starting the second line at the edge of the ruler, so it is a little too long.

start.text: Mei wants a line 8 cm long. She puts the 0 mark at the start and draws to the 7 mark. She says: my line is 8 cm. Is she right?

parts.text: Yes or no? ___
Her line is ___ cm long.

start.answer: No. Her line is 7 cm. She should draw on to the 8 mark
start.hint: Where does her line end on the ruler? Look at the mark. What mark should it end at?
start.solution: Mei started at 0 and stopped at the 7 mark, so her line is 7 cm long. A line 8 cm long must end at the 8 mark. She should draw on to the 8 mark.
mistakes: Saying yes because she wanted 8.
Counting the 0 as one, so the 7 mark looked like 8.

start.text: The tip of Ben's spoon is between the 14 mark and the 15 mark. It is closer to the 15 mark. The spoon starts at the 0 mark.

parts.text: To the nearest cm, the spoon is ___ cm long.

start.answer: 15 cm (the tip is closer to the 15 mark)
start.hint: Which mark is the tip closer to? That mark is the length to the nearest centimetre.
start.solution: The tip is between 14 and 15 and it is closer to 15. So, to the nearest centimetre, the spoon is 15 cm long.
mistakes: Writing 14 because the tip has not reached 15.
Writing 14 and a half.

think.text: Mei draws a path with 3 straight pieces: 5 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. Draw the path in the box with your ruler. How long is the whole path?

parts.text: The whole path is ___ cm long.

think.hint: Draw one piece at a time. Turn a corner and draw the next piece. Then add the three lengths.
think.solution: Draw 5 cm, turn, draw 3 cm, turn, draw 4 cm. The path is as long as all three pieces together: 5 + 3 = 8, and 8 + 4 = 12 cm.
mistakes: Measuring in a straight line from the start to the end of the path.
Drawing one long line instead of turning at the corners.

think.text: A line starts at the 2 mark of a ruler and ends at the 9 mark. A second line starts at the 3 mark and is 6 cm long.

parts.text: The first line is ___ cm long.
The second line ends at the ___ mark.

think.hint: Count the jumps from the start mark to the end mark. For the second line, jump 6 along from the 3 mark.
think.solution: (a) From the 2 mark to the 9 mark is 7 jumps: 9 take away 2 is 7 cm, not 9 cm. (b) Start at the 3 mark and jump on 6: 3 + 6 = 9. The line ends at the 9 mark.
mistakes: Writing 9 for the first line because the end is at the 9 mark.
Taking 6 away from 3, or writing 6 for the second answer.

think.text: Draw a line 13 cm long in the box. Put a dot on it 5 cm from the start.

parts.text: The dot is ___ cm from the end of the line.

think.hint: The whole line is 13 cm. The first part is 5 cm. How many cm are left? You can check by measuring from the dot to the end.
think.solution: The whole line is 13 cm and the part before the dot is 5 cm. The rest is 13 take away 5, which is 8 cm. Check by measuring from the dot to the end of the line.
mistakes: Writing 5, the part that is already known.
Adding 13 + 5 = 18.

think.text: Both pencils start at 0. To the nearest cm: Ali's tip is between the 16 and 17 marks, closer to 16. Mei's tip is between the 18 and 19 marks, closer to 19.

parts.text: Ali: ___ cm. Mei: ___ cm. Mei's is ___ cm longer.

think.hint: For each pencil, choose the mark that the tip is closer to. Then find how much longer by counting on from 16 to 19.
think.solution: Ali's tip is closer to 16, so 16 cm. Mei's tip is closer to 19, so 19 cm. From 16 to 19 is 3 jumps, so Mei's pencil is 3 cm longer.
mistakes: Choosing the mark the tip has already passed (17 and 18).
Writing 2 by using 17 and 19.

go.text: A ribbon is 30 cm long. Mei cuts it into three pieces. Piece A is 8 cm long. Piece B is 3 cm longer than piece A. How long is piece C?
go.answer: Piece C is 11 cm (B is 11 cm, A and B together are 19 cm, and 30 take away 19 is 11)
go.hint: Find piece B first. Then add A and B. How much of the 30 cm is left for C?
go.solution: B is 8 + 3 = 11 cm. A and B together are 8 + 11 = 19 cm. The ribbon is 30 cm, so C is 30 take away 19, which is 11 cm. Check: 8 + 11 + 11 = 30.
mistakes: Taking 30 - 8 = 22 and stopping.
Writing 3 for piece B instead of 3 more than A.

go.text: A snail starts at the 4 mark of a long ruler. It crawls to the 13 mark. Then it crawls back 5 cm towards the 0 mark.

parts.text: The snail is now at the ___ mark.
In all, the snail has crawled ___ cm.

go.answer: At the 8 mark; it crawled 14 cm in all (9 cm forward and 5 cm back)
go.hint: Forward: from 4 to 13 is how many cm? Back: take 5 from the 13 mark. For the total, add the way forward and the way back.
go.solution: Forward from the 4 mark to the 13 mark is 9 cm. Back 5 cm: 13 take away 5 puts the snail at the 8 mark. In all it crawled 9 + 5 = 14 cm, although it is only 4 cm from where it began.
mistakes: Writing 9 for the total and forgetting the way back.
Writing 4 as the mark (the distance from the start, not the mark).

go.text: Draw a path with 3 straight pieces. Every piece must be a different whole number of cm long. The whole path must be exactly 20 cm. Write the 3 lengths.

parts.text: My 3 lengths: ___ cm, ___ cm and ___ cm.

go.answer: Any 3 different whole numbers that add up to 20, for example 5, 7 and 8 (5 + 7 + 8 = 20)
go.hint: Pick 3 different numbers and add them. Too small? Make one longer. Too big? Make one shorter. Then draw each piece.
go.solution: One answer is 5, 7 and 8: 5 + 7 is 12 and 12 + 8 is 20. Other answers are 3, 8 and 9, or 4, 7 and 9. If the total is not 20, change one piece until it is.
mistakes: Two pieces the same length (for example 5, 5 and 10).
A total of 19 or 21 because a piece was drawn a little too long or too short.

investigation.title: Does the start mark matter?
investigation.first: Draw a line 6 cm long. Put the 2 mark of your ruler at its start. Which mark is at its end?
investigation.text: Try 3 start marks. Is the length always the same? Is there a rule?
investigation.answer: The length stays 6 cm every time. From the 2 mark the line ends at 8; from 3 it ends at 9; from 5 it ends at 11. The end mark is always the start mark plus 6, so the end mark take away the start mark is always 6. Reading only the end mark gives the length only when the line starts at 0.
investigation.look_for: A child who tries more than one start mark, writes both marks, and says that the end mark take away the start mark (or the number of jumps) is the length. A 15 cm ruler allows start marks up to 9.
mistakes: Writing the end mark as the length (8 for a line from 2 to 8).
Trying only one start mark.

talk.question: Mei measures a pencil and says it is 15 cm. Ben measures the same pencil and says it is 16 cm. What could have happened? How can we find out who is right?
talk.answer: The tip may be between the 15 mark and the 16 mark, so one child chose the other mark. Or one child did not start at the 0 mark. We can check by measuring again with the 0 mark at the start, and by choosing the closer mark.
talk.look_for: A reason about the start at 0 or about an end between two marks, and a way to check (measure again). Praise the check, not who is right.

exit.text: Draw a line 6 cm long on your spare paper. Then write where it starts and ends on your ruler.

parts.text: It starts at the ___ mark and ends at the ___ mark.

exit.answer: A line from the 0 mark to the 6 mark
exit.solution: Put the 0 mark of the ruler on the dot and draw to the 6 mark. The line starts at 0 and ends at 6.
mistakes: Starting at the edge of the ruler.
Ending at the 7 mark after counting the 0 as one.

exit.text: Siti's eraser ends at the 6 mark and her pencil ends at the 15 mark. Both start at 0.

parts.text: The pencil is ___ cm longer than the eraser.

exit.solution: The eraser is 6 cm and the pencil is 15 cm. 15 take away 6 is 9, so the pencil is 9 cm longer.
mistakes: Adding: 21.
Writing 15 (the pencil, not the difference).

exit.text: A line starts at the 3 mark and ends at the 10 mark. How long is the line?

parts.text: The line is ___ cm long.

exit.answer: 7 cm. 10 take away 3 is 7 (7 jumps from 3 to 10)
exit.solution: Count the jumps from 3 to 10: 7 jumps. Or take 10 take away 3, which is 7. The line is 7 cm long, not 10 cm.
mistakes: Writing 10 (the end mark).
Writing 13 by adding.

hardest: a line that starts at another mark
adding the pieces of a path

home_practice.text: Draw a line 8 cm long on spare paper. On your ruler, where does it start? Where does it end?
home_practice.answer: It starts at 0 and ends at 8
home_practice.solution: A line 8 cm long, drawn from the 0 mark, ends at the 8 mark.

home_practice.text: A pencil starts at the 0 mark and its tip is at the 17 mark. A crayon is 11 cm long. How much longer is the pencil?
home_practice.solution: The pencil is 17 cm. 17 take away 11 is 6 (count on from 11 to 17: 6 jumps).

home_practice.text: Measure a spoon, a toy and a book to the nearest cm. Write the lengths from shortest to longest.
home_practice.answer: Any three lengths, written from smallest to largest. A grown-up can check one by measuring again
home_practice.solution: Put one end at the 0 mark and read the mark at the other end. If the end is between two marks, write the closer one. Then put the numbers in order.

home_practice.text: A line starts at the 4 mark and ends at the 15 mark. How long is the line? Show how you know.
home_practice.solution: Count the jumps from 4 to 15: 11 jumps. Or take 4 from 15, which is 11. It is not 15 cm, because the line starts at the 4 mark.

home_practice.text: At home: draw a path with 3 different straight pieces that is 25 cm long in all. Write each length. A grown-up checks with a ruler.
home_practice.answer: Any 3 different whole numbers that add up to 25, for example 6, 8 and 11 (6 + 8 + 11 = 25)
home_practice.solution: Choose three different numbers that add to 25, draw each piece with the 0 mark at the start, then measure and add to check.

items.q: A pencil starts at the 0 mark of a ruler. Its tip is at the 12 mark. How long is the pencil in cm?
items.hint: The pencil starts at 0, so the mark at the tip is the length.
steps: The pencil starts at the 0 mark.
The tip is at the 12 mark.
So the pencil is 12 cm long.

slips.say: 13 counts the 0 mark as one centimetre. The first centimetre is from 0 to 1, so the tip mark is the length.

tpl.q: A pencil starts at the 0 mark of a ruler. Its tip is at the {n} mark. How long is the pencil in cm?
tpl.hint: The pencil starts at 0, so the mark at the tip is the length.
steps: The pencil starts at the 0 mark.
The tip is at the {n} mark.
So the pencil is {ans} cm long.

items.q: Ali's line is 12 cm long. Mei's line is 5 cm long. How much longer is Ali's line?
items.hint: Count on from the short line to the long line, or take the short length from the long length.
steps: Ali's line is 12 cm. Mei's line is 5 cm.
Count on from 5 to 12, or take 5 from 12.
Ali's line is 7 cm longer.

slips.say: 17 adds the two lengths. How much longer needs the gap between them: take away.
12 is Ali's whole line. How much more than Mei's line is it?

tpl.q: Ali's line is {a} cm long. Mei's line is {b} cm long. How much longer is Ali's line?
tpl.hint: Count on from {b} to {a}, or take {b} from {a}.
steps: Ali's line is {a} cm. Mei's line is {b} cm.
Find the gap: take {b} from {a}.
Ali's line is {ans} cm longer.

items.q: You are going to draw a line 6 cm long. Where do you put the 0 mark of your ruler?
options: On the dot where the line starts
On the dot where the line ends
items.answer: On the dot where the line starts
items.hint: The 0 mark is where we start counting centimetres.
steps: We count centimetres from the 0 mark.
So the 0 mark goes on the dot where the line starts.
Then make a small mark at the 6 and join them.

slips.say: If the 0 is not at the start, the line will not be 6 cm long unless you take the start mark away.

items.q: Mei draws a line 5 cm long. Then she draws a second line 3 cm longer than the first. How long is the second line?
items.hint: The second line is the first line and 3 more.
steps: The first line is 5 cm.
3 cm longer means 5 + 3.
The second line is 8 cm long.

slips.say: 3 is how much longer it is. The second line is the whole 5 cm and 3 more.
2 is 5 - 3. Longer means add.

tpl.q: Mei draws a line {a} cm long. Then she draws a second line {d} cm longer than the first. How long is the second line?
tpl.hint: The second line is the first line and {d} more.
steps: The first line is {a} cm.
{d} cm longer means {a} + {d}.
The second line is {ans} cm long.

items.q: The tip of a spoon is between the 14 mark and the 15 mark, closer to the 15 mark. The spoon starts at 0. How long is the spoon to the nearest cm?
items.hint: Which mark is the tip closer to?
steps: The tip is between 14 and 15.
It is closer to 15.
To the nearest centimetre the spoon is 15 cm long.

slips.say: 14 is the mark the tip has passed, but it is closer to 15.

tpl.q: The tip of a spoon is between the {m} mark and the {k} mark, closer to the {k} mark. The spoon starts at 0. How long is the spoon to the nearest cm?
tpl.hint: Which mark is the tip closer to?
steps: The tip is between {m} and {k}.
It is closer to {k}.
To the nearest centimetre the spoon is {ans} cm long.

items.q: A line starts at the 2 mark and ends at the 9 mark. How long is the line in cm?
items.hint: Count the jumps from the start mark to the end mark.
steps: The line starts at the 2 mark, not at 0.
Count the jumps from 2 to 9, or take 2 from 9.
The line is 7 cm long.

slips.say: 9 is the end mark. The line starts at 2, so the first 2 cm are not part of it.
11 adds the marks. Take the start from the end.

tpl.q: A line starts at the {s} mark and ends at the {e} mark. How long is the line in cm?
tpl.hint: Count the jumps from {s} to {e}, or take {s} from {e}.
steps: The line starts at the {s} mark, not at 0.
Take {s} from {e}.
The line is {ans} cm long.

items.q: A path has 3 straight pieces: 5 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. How long is the whole path?
steps: Add the first two pieces: 5 + 3 = 8.
Add the third piece: 8 + 4 = 12.
The path is 12 cm long.

slips.say: 5 is only the first piece. The path is all three pieces joined.

tpl.q: A path has 3 straight pieces: {a} cm, {b} cm and {c} cm. How long is the whole path?
steps: Add the first two pieces: {a} + {b}.
Then add the third piece: {c}.
The path is {ans} cm long.

items.q: A line starts at the 3 mark and is 6 cm long. At which mark does it end?
items.hint: Jump 6 along the ruler from the 3 mark.
steps: The line starts at the 3 mark.
It is 6 cm long, so jump on 6.
3 + 6 = 9. It ends at the 9 mark.

slips.say: 6 is the length. The line starts at 3, so the end mark is 6 more than 3.
3 is where the line starts. Where does it end?

tpl.q: A line starts at the {s} mark and is {l} cm long. At which mark does it end?
tpl.hint: Jump {l} along the ruler from the {s} mark.
steps: The line starts at the {s} mark.
It is {l} cm long, so jump on {l}.
It ends at the {ans} mark.

items.q: Ben starts a line at the 2 mark and it ends at the 9 mark. He says: it is 9 cm long. Is he right?
items.hint: The line starts at 2. Count the jumps from 2 to 9.
steps: The line starts at the 2 mark, not at 0.
Count the jumps from 2 to 9: 7 jumps.
So the line is 7 cm long.

slips.say: The first 2 cm of the ruler are not part of his line. Count the jumps from 2.
11 adds 2 and 9. Take the start from the end instead.

items.q: A ribbon is 30 cm long. Piece A is 8 cm. Piece B is 3 cm longer than piece A. How long is piece C, the rest of the ribbon?
items.hint: Find piece B first. Then see how much of the 30 cm is left.
steps: Piece B is 8 + 3 = 11 cm.
A and B together are 8 + 11 = 19 cm.
C is 30 take away 19, which is 11 cm.

slips.say: 22 is 30 - 8. Piece B is also cut from the ribbon.
3 is how much longer B is than A, not the length of C.

tpl.q: A ribbon is {T} cm long. Piece A is {a} cm. Piece B is {d} cm longer than piece A. How long is piece C, the rest of the ribbon?
tpl.hint: Find piece B first. Then see how much of the {T} cm is left.
steps: Piece B is {a} + {d} = {b} cm.
A and B together are {ab} cm.
C is {T} take away {ab}, which is {ans} cm.

items.q: A snail starts at the 4 mark of a long ruler. It crawls to the 13 mark. Then it crawls back 5 cm. In all, how far has the snail crawled?
items.hint: Find the way forward. Then add the way back.
steps: Forward from 4 to 13 is 9 cm.
Then back 5 cm.
In all: 9 + 5 = 14 cm.

slips.say: 9 is only the way forward. Add the way back too.
4 is where the snail began. The question asks how far it crawled.

tpl.q: A snail starts at the {s} mark of a long ruler. It crawls to the {e} mark. Then it crawls back {b} cm. In all, how far has the snail crawled?
tpl.hint: Find the way forward. Then add the way back.
steps: Forward from {s} to {e} is {f} cm.
Then back {b} cm.
In all: {f} + {b} = {ans} cm.

items.q: A strip of paper is 10 cm long. You may cut it at a mark: the 1 mark, the 2 mark and so on, but not at the two ends. How many different places can you cut?
items.hint: Which marks are inside the strip, not at the ends?
steps: The marks are 0, 1, 2, up to 10.
The 0 mark and the 10 mark are the ends.
So you can cut at the marks 1 to 9: 9 places.

slips.say: The 10 mark is the end of the strip. Cutting there makes no new piece.
11 counts every mark from 0 to 10. Cuts are only inside the strip.

tpl.q: A strip of paper is {n} cm long. You may cut it at a mark: the 1 mark, the 2 mark and so on, but not at the two ends. How many different places can you cut?
tpl.hint: Which marks are inside the strip, not at the ends?
steps: The marks go from 0 to {n}.
The 0 mark and the {n} mark are the ends.
You can cut at the marks in between: {ans} places.

items.q: Make up your own path puzzle: 3 straight pieces that are all different and add up to exactly 20 cm. Check by adding.
items.hint: Pick 3 different numbers first. Add them. Change one until the total is 20.
steps: Pick 3 different whole numbers.
Add them. If the total is not 20, make one piece longer or shorter.
For example 5, 7 and 8: 5 + 7 + 8 = 20. Then draw the path and measure each piece.

parent.summary: We learned to use a ruler properly. Your child measured things from home, drew lines up to 12 cm and compared lengths. The big idea: start at the 0 mark, read the mark at the other end, and when the end falls between two marks choose the closer one. We also met a line that starts at a different mark.
parent.quote: Start at the 0 mark. Read the mark at the other end. Between two marks? Choose the closer one.
words: centimetre (cm): the gap between two marks
path: straight pieces joined at corners
try_home: Measure it: find 5 things. Your child guesses each length, then measures to the nearest centimetre. Put them in order, shortest first.
Draw it: say a length such as 9 cm and let your child draw it. Swap: you draw, your child measures. Start at the edge on purpose, for them to spot.
Spot it: look at a tape measure or a growth chart. Ask: where is the 0? How many centimetres from here to there?
ask: What if the end is between two marks?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child slide a finger along the ruler and count the jumps aloud. Wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking "where is your 0?" works better than giving the answer.
parent.next: Lesson 10: Story Steps: Read It Twice. Your child needs a pencil and paper only.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to measure and draw lines to the nearest centimetre with a ruler and to say how they know. This week: starting at 0, reading the end mark, and comparing lengths.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why.

safeguarding: Rulers stay flat on the table when not in use: no swinging, no flicking, no pointing. Plastic or wooden rulers only, no metal edges, no compasses. Small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Sneak-peek and exit answers are shown on the child's own paper to the camera at the same moment, once. There is no private chat and no board held up in front of the group. When asked to show a ruler or a thing, the child holds it to the camera: the tutor looks at the ruler and the paper, not at the child.
Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. Never show a child's page in the recording; record the tutor and the screen only, with children's video excluded.
A child who ticks "I am still stuck" gets a check-in in the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared room or a hand signal, parent nearby). No private messages to children.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself with a real ruler first. Check that question 3 and the pencil examples work with your own pencil.

Tell parents a week before: a ruler marked in centimetres starting at 0, workbook pages 1 to 5 printed on A4 (page 6, the cut-out page, is not used in this lesson), about 4 things to measure, 10 paper clips or small same-size things, a pencil and spare paper.
Have your own ruler, a pencil and a strip of paper ready, and a camera that can look down at the table. Have the slides open and check the clock or timer is visible on screen share.
Check the recording settings exclude children's video. If a family has no ruler, ask them before the lesson so a grown-up can find one; do not ask the child in front of the group.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask "How do you know?" and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: a line that ends at the 9 mark is always 9 cm long. Is that always true? Draw lines that end at the 9 mark and start at 0, at 2 and at 4. Measure each one.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Draw 3 lines that all end at the 9 mark: one starts at 0, one at 2, one at 4. How long is each?
menu.answer: Not always. A line that starts at 0 and ends at 9 is 9 cm. Starting at 2 it is 7 cm, and starting at 4 it is 5 cm. It is only true when the line starts at the 0 mark.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Draw a path with 3 straight pieces. Write the total length on the back, but not the pieces. Give it to your grown-up to measure each piece and add them. Do they get your total?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Draw a path with 3 straight pieces. Ask a grown-up to measure and add them. Does it match your total?
menu.answer: No single answer. The measured pieces should add up to the total on the back, give or take 1 cm from reading the nearest centimetre.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never used a ruler. Teach them how to draw a line 9 cm long, step by step, and say why the 0 mark goes on the dot.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to draw a line 9 cm long with a ruler, in steps.
menu.answer: A dot for the start. The 0 mark on the dot. A small mark at the 9. Join them with a straight line. Check: 0 at the start, 9 at the end. We start at 0 because the centimetres are counted from the 0 mark.
